newsitem.title: USA: UAW sets strike deadline at GM Cadillac plant.
newsitem.headline: UAW sets strike deadline at GM Cadillac plant.

text.p: The United Auto Workers set another strike deadline at General Motors Corp. on Friday, this time selecting the Cadillac assembly plant that is set to start production of the 1998 Seville this fall.

UAW Local 22 notified GM it may go on strike at 11:59 p.m. EDT (0359 GMT) on Aug. 8, if a new contract is not reached by then. The local has about 3,500 members at the plant in Detroit's Hamtramck neighbourhood.

The facility is GM's only luxury car facility, producing the Cadillac Eldorado, Seville and Deville/Concours. This month, it is scheduled to start production of the Buick Park Avenue, which is also made at GM's Orion Township, Mich., plant.

UAW spokesman Reg McGhee said the disputes between GM and UAW Local 22 are over staffing levels, health and safety concerns and subcontracting issues. They are many of the same issues that have plagued contract talks all year between GM and its locals, leading to six strikes since January against the world's largest automaker.

GM settled a three-day strike July 25 at an engine and transmission plant in Warren, Mich., that had forced GM to shut down six car assembly plants and idle 16,500 workers. Including the Cadillac plant, there are nine of GM's 105 UAW locals without new contracts.
Analysts said a strike at the Cadillac facility would take about two weeks to affect sales, but it could impact other GM parts plants sooner.
"This is an important facility, it builds all your luxury cars," said Michael Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting, an industry consultant in Farmington Hills, Mich.
Robinet said the Cadillac plant is a big recipient of parts from GM's stamping plant in Grand Blanc, Mich., and a powertrain facility in Ypsilanti, Mich.

The Cadillac plant is to start production of the 1998 Seville in October. GM will unveil the car at the Frankfurt auto show in September and begin sales in January. The new Seville has been redesigned and is considered a key product for GM as it pushes further into the global luxury car market.

GM has enough inventory of existing models to withstand a two-week strike at the facility, said Christopher Cedergren of industry consultant Nextrend in Thousand Oaks, Calif. But beyond that a work stoppage could take a bite out of Cadillac's 1998 model year sales.
"Generally speaking, Cadillac does well in October and November because most traditional Cadillac buyers like to buy at the beginning of the model year," he said.

GM and the UAW signed a national labour contract in November. But the company has run into resistance from union locals as it seeks to shrink its work force through attrition and send more work to outside suppliers.
